reason: Backshift is not automatic: u25 itself says a past stays put, a Trieste handout gives Dijo que había tenido/tuvo un accidente, and Google Ngrams has dijo que fue at about 3 to 4 against dijo que había sido (NGLE from memory only). Verbs do not step back in place, so the wording changed, and it takes in LC-029's Bogotá example so the rule says this once.
quote: When you retell a conversation after the fact, everything takes one step back, in time and in place. Spanish does it as faithfully as English.
replacement: When you retell a conversation after the fact, most things take one step back, in time and in place, just as in English. Two things can stop that. If what was said still holds right now, the verb can stay: *Dijo que Bogotá es fría*, or *Dijo que viene mañana* if tomorrow has not come yet. And a plain past often stays as it is: *Dijo que ya habló con ellos.*

quote: Keep the two halves in the same time. A word like *ayer* or *el año pasado* tells you to go to the second pair. You may also mix them on purpose: a past "if" with a result about today, as in *Si hubiera aceptado, hoy viviría en Toronto.*
replacement: The two halves usually share a time. A word like *ayer* or *el año pasado* tells you to go to the second pair. You can also mix them on purpose. A past "if" with a result about today: *Si hubiera aceptado, hoy viviría en Toronto.* A lasting "if" with a result in the past: *Si fuera más paciente, no habría dicho eso.*

replacement: Teachers call this the conditional of rumour, or *condicional de rumor*, and in journalism it is a way of reporting without taking responsibility for the claim. Many newspaper style guides discourage it, so learn to read it and be careful about writing it.
